lessons.title: Five Ways to Explore
objectives: Name the five senses and the body part for each
Use the senses to describe an object
explanation: We have five senses that tell us about the world. We see with our eyes, hear with our ears, smell with our nose, taste with our tongue, and touch with our skin.
Our senses work together. When we eat a mango, we see its yellow colour, smell its sweet smell, feel its smooth skin and taste its juicy sweetness.
Our senses help keep us safe too: we smell smoke, hear a car horn, and feel when something is too hot.

objectives: Name ways to protect eyes, ears and skin

explanation: Our senses are precious, so we look after them. Never look straight at the Sun. Take breaks from screens and look at faraway things to rest your eyes.
Very loud sounds can hurt our ears. We can cover our ears near very loud noises and keep the volume low on headphones.

Some people use glasses to see better or hearing aids to hear better. Some people who are blind read Braille with their fingers, and some people who are deaf talk using sign language. Everyone senses the world in their own way.

lessons.title: The Taste Test
objectives: Name the basic tastes
Show that smell helps us taste
explanation: Your tongue has taste buds that sense five basic tastes: sweet (sugar), salty (salt), sour (lemon), bitter (karela, bitter gourd), and umami — a savoury taste found in foods like tomatoes and mushrooms.
Smell and taste work together. Much of what we call "flavour" actually comes from smell!
When you have a blocked nose from a cold, food tastes bland because your nose can't help.

context.text: The old "tongue map" showing different tastes in different zones is a myth; taste buds across the tongue can sense all basic tastes.

lessons.title: Why Two Ears?
objectives: Describe textures using touch words
Explain why two ears help find where a sound comes from
explanation: Our skin can feel textures — rough, smooth, soft, bumpy, prickly — and also temperature: hot and cold. Fingertips are especially sensitive.

Having two ears helps us tell where a sound comes from. A sound on your left reaches your left ear a tiny bit earlier and a little louder than your right ear. Your brain uses this to work out the direction.
With one ear covered, finding the direction of a sound is much harder.

lessons.title: Inside the Eye
objectives: Name parts of the eye
Explain that we see when light enters our eyes
prerequisites: Knows light travels in straight lines
explanation: We see things because light bounces off them and enters our eyes. Light passes through the pupil — the black hole in the middle of the eye.
The coloured part around it is the iris, which makes the pupil bigger in dim light and smaller in bright light. The lens focuses light onto the retina at the back of the eye.
The retina sends signals along the optic nerve to the brain, which turns them into the pictures we see. Glasses help focus light properly when the eye's lens can't do it alone.

lessons.title: A Sound's Journey
objectives: Trace how sound travels through the ear
Explain how loud noise can damage hearing
explanation: Sound is made by vibrations travelling through the air. The outer ear collects sound and funnels it into the ear canal.

The vibrations hit the eardrum, a thin skin that vibrates too. Three tiny bones (the smallest in the body) pass the vibrations to the cochlea, a snail-shaped part filled with liquid and tiny hair cells.
The hair cells turn vibrations into signals sent to the brain. Very loud sounds can damage these hair cells, and they don't grow back — so protecting hearing matters.

vocabulary.meaning: a thin skin that vibrates with sound
a snail-shaped part of the inner ear
shaking back and forth
a unit for how loud a sound is

examples: The stapes, in the middle ear, is the smallest bone in the body.

lessons.title: Optical Illusions
objectives: Explain that perception is the brain's interpretation
Investigate several illusions
explanation: Your eyes collect light, but your brain decides what you see. This is called perception. Usually it's accurate — but sometimes the brain makes mistakes we call illusions.
In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two equal lines look different lengths because of arrow-shaped ends. Afterimages appear when you stare at a colour, then look at white.
Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina and there are no light sensors. You don't notice it because your brain fills in the gap!

vocabulary.meaning: how the brain interprets sensory information

a part of the retina with no light sensors

examples: Equal lines looking unequal.

lessons.title: Our Hidden Senses
objectives: Name senses beyond the traditional five
Explain balance and body-position senses
explanation: The "five senses" idea is old and simple. Scientists recognise more. The vestibular sense, in your inner ear, tells you about balance and movement — that's why spinning makes you dizzy.
Proprioception tells you where your body parts are without looking — you can touch your nose with your eyes closed.
We also sense temperature, pain, hunger, thirst and the need to breathe. These internal senses help keep us safe and healthy.

lessons.title: Senses We Don't Have

explanation: Bees can see ultraviolet light, revealing patterns on flowers invisible to us. Some snakes, like pit vipers, detect infrared heat from warm-blooded prey.
Many migrating birds appear to sense Earth's magnetic field. Sharks detect weak electric fields made by other animals' muscles.
Humans use technology to extend our senses: microscopes and telescopes for sight, infrared cameras for heat, microphones and sonar for sound, and sensors for magnetic fields.

lessons.title: Universal Design
objectives: Describe assistive technologies for sensory disabilities
Apply universal design principles to a space or product
explanation: Millions of people live with visual or hearing impairments. Disability is shaped not only by the body but by the environment: a building without ramps disables wheelchair users; a video without captions excludes deaf viewers.

Assistive technologies include screen readers that speak text aloud, Braille displays, hearing aids, cochlear implants, captions and sign-language interpreters. Tactile paving helps blind people navigate pavements and stations.
Universal design creates spaces and products usable by as many people as possible from the start — benefiting everyone, like captions that help in noisy places.

context.text: India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, recognises a range of disabilities and requires accessibility in public buildings, transport and information.

vocabulary.meaning: how easily people of all abilities can use something

examples: Audio announcements and Braille signage in metro stations.

story.text: A museum asked blind and deaf visitors to test its exhibits. They found tiny labels, no audio guides, and videos without captions. After redesigning with tactile models, audio descriptions and captions, visitor numbers rose for everyone — families loved touching the models too.

lessons.title: How Neurons Talk
objectives: Describe neuron structure and signal transmission
Explain synapses and neurotransmitters
explanation: Neurons are cells specialised to carry electrical signals. Dendrites receive signals, the cell body processes them, and a long axon carries the signal (an action potential) to other cells. A fatty myelin sheath speeds transmission.
Between neurons is a tiny gap called a synapse. When a signal arrives, chemicals called neurotransmitters cross the gap and trigger the next neuron.
The human brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons with trillions of connections. Learning strengthens some connections — neuroplasticity.

vocabulary.meaning: a nerve cell
the long fibre carrying signals away from the cell body
the gap between neurons
a chemical that carries signals across synapses
the brain's ability to change with experience

examples: Practising a skill strengthens neural pathways.

story.title: Cajal's Drawings
story.text: In the late 1800s, Santiago Ramón y Cajal stained brain tissue and spent years drawing neurons under a microscope. He argued that the brain was made of separate cells connected at tiny gaps — not one continuous net. His beautiful drawings are still used, and he shared a Nobel Prize in 1906.

units.title: The Puzzle of Experience
units.summary: How does the brain make the world we experience?
objectives: Explain perception as an active, predictive process

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Is the World Inside Your Head?
objectives: Explain perception as an active, predictive process
Discuss scientific and philosophical views of consciousness
explanation: Modern neuroscience suggests the brain doesn't just record the world — it predicts it, using past experience to make best guesses, then corrects them with sensory input.
Attention matters: in a famous experiment, many viewers counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene — inattentional blindness.

Why physical brain activity produces subjective experience — the redness of red, the taste of mango — is called "the hard problem of consciousness". Scientists, philosophers and religious traditions (including Indian schools of thought on consciousness, or chit) approach it in different ways, and it remains open.

context.text: The "invisible gorilla" study by Simons and Chabris (1999) demonstrated inattentional blindness.

Positions on consciousness range from physicalism (it arises from brain processes) to views that consciousness is fundamental; Advaita Vedanta, for example, holds consciousness to be the ultimate reality. These are presented as differing perspectives.

vocabulary.meaning: the idea that the brain predicts sensory input
failing to notice something unexpected when attention is elsewhere
subjective awareness
why physical processes give rise to experience

examples: Missing a friend waving while focused on your phone.
Hearing your name in a noisy room (the cocktail party effect).

story.title: The Invisible Gorilla
story.text: Students watched a video and counted passes between players in white shirts. Afterwards, the teacher asked, "Did you see the gorilla?" Half the class laughed — "What gorilla?" On replay, a person in a gorilla suit walked right through the middle, thumping their chest. Attention had shaped what they saw.
